related_questions.question: How does a PARP inhibitor work?

text_blocks.snippet: PARP inhibitors are a type of targeted therapy used to treat certain cancers by blocking a protein called PARP, which helps cancer cells repair damaged DNA. By inhibiting PARP, these drugs prevent cancer cells with broken DNA from repairing themselves, ultimately leading to cell death. They are particularly effective against cancers with mutations in genes like BRCA, which are involved in DNA repair.
snippet_highlighted_words: blocking a protein called PARP, which helps cancer cells repair damaged DNA

list.title: What is PARP?
list.snippet: PARP, or poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase, is an enzyme that plays a crucial role in DNA repair within cells. When DNA is damaged, PARP helps to fix it, allowing the cell to survive.

list.title: How PARP inhibitors work:
list.snippet: PARP inhibitors essentially sabotage this repair process by blocking the PARP enzyme. This means that cancer cells with damaged DNA can't fix themselves, leading to cell death.

list.title: BRCA mutations and PARP inhibitors:
list.snippet: PARP inhibitors are particularly effective against cancers with BRCA mutations (BRCA1 or BRCA2). These mutations weaken the cell's ability to repair DNA damage, making them more vulnerable to PARP inhibitors.

list.title: Other DNA repair deficiencies:
list.snippet: Besides BRCA mutations, PARP inhibitors can also be effective in cancers with other DNA repair deficiencies.

list.title: Types of cancers treated:
list.snippet: PARP inhibitors are used to treat various cancers, including breast, ovarian, prostate, and pancreatic cancers.

list.title: Examples of PARP inhibitors:
list.snippet: Several PARP inhibitors are approved for use, including olaparib, talazoparib, rucaparib, and niraparib.

list.title: Side effects:
list.snippet: Like all cancer treatments, PARP inhibitors can cause side effects, such as anemia, nausea, and fatigue.

list.title: Targeted therapy:
list.snippet: PARP inhibitors are a type of targeted therapy, meaning they aim to specifically target cancer cells while minimizing harm to healthy cells.

text_blocks.snippet: PARP inhibitors are a type of targeted therapy used to treat ovarian cancer, particularly in cases where the cancer has a BRCA mutation or homologous recombination deficiency (HRD). These inhibitors work by blocking a protein called PARP, which helps cancer cells repair damaged DNA. By inhibiting PARP, these drugs can cause cancer cells to die, especially those with impaired DNA repair mechanisms like BRCA mutations.
snippet_highlighted_words: a type of targeted therapy used to treat ovarian cancer, particularly in cases where the cancer has a BRCA mutation or homologous recombination deficiency (HRD)

list.snippet: PARP (Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase) is an enzyme involved in DNA repair.
PARP inhibitors are drugs that block PARP's activity, preventing cancer cells from repairing DNA damage.
This is particularly effective against cancer cells that already have difficulty repairing DNA, like those with BRCA mutations.

text_blocks.snippet: 2. How do PARP inhibitors work in ovarian cancer?

list.snippet: Many ovarian cancers, especially those with BRCA mutations, have a compromised ability to repair DNA damage through a process called homologous recombination (HR).
PARP inhibitors exploit this weakness by preventing cancer cells from using PARP to repair DNA damage.
This leads to the accumulation of DNA damage and ultimately, the death of cancer cells.

text_blocks.snippet: 3. Types of PARP inhibitors used in ovarian cancer:

list.snippet: Several PARP inhibitors are approved for treating ovarian cancer, including olaparib, rucaparib, and niraparib.
These drugs are often used as maintenance therapy after initial chemotherapy, helping to keep the cancer from returning.
Patients with BRCA mutations are often the most responsive to PARP inhibitors.
However, PARP inhibitors can also be effective in some patients with HRD even without a BRCA mutation.
HRD can be identified through molecular testing.
Platinum-sensitive patients may also benefit from PARP inhibitors, according to the Journal of Ovarian Research.
Can significantly reduce the risk of ovarian cancer recurrence, with some studies showing a reduction of up to 70%.
May improve progression-free survival (the time before the cancer worsens), according to a study published in the Journal of Ovarian Research.
Common side effects include fatigue, nausea, and anemia.
Some patients may experience other side effects like diarrhea, taste changes, headaches, or dizziness.
In rare cases (1-2%), PARP inhibitors can lead to acute myeloid leukemia.
Tumors can develop resistance to PARP inhibitors, meaning the treatment becomes less effective over time.
Various mechanisms of resistance have been identified in research.
